792.title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
792.hook: Jewish tradition reads the servant as the people Israel in exile
792.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 52 and 53 as part of the book of Isaiah; Jewish commentators read the servant as the people Israel, and the passage is part of the conversation between Jews and Christians, who read it differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a city said she'd been forgotten, and heard: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands. Your line was you are in the palm.

Somebody in this chapter is speaking, and they sound stunned. Kings shut their mouths. A voice asks, Who hath believed our report? And then a group starts to confess. We looked at him and saw nothing worth seeing. We turned our faces away. We thought he was struck down by God. But he was wounded for what we had done. Isaiah fifty-three is written mostly in the voice of onlookers, realizing too late what they did to someone they despised. The question it leaves: who is the someone? And who are we?
screen: `KINGS SHUT THEIR MOUTHS.` → `A GROUP STARTS TO CONFESS.` → `WHO IS HE? WHO ARE WE?`

segments.voice: The onlookers describe him: "He was despised, and forsaken of men, A man of pains, and acquainted with disease." Wounded, bruised, led like a lamb, cut off, and yet in the end, the chapter says, he shall see his seed and prolong his days. So who is this servant? Jewish tradition answers from inside the book of Isaiah itself. A few chapters earlier, the prophet names the servant outright: "Thou art My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." And again: But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen. Read that way, the servant in chapter fifty-three is the people Israel in exile: scattered, mocked, treated as if their suffering proved God had abandoned them. And the we who speak are the nations, the kings who shut their mouths, finally seeing that the people they scorned carried more than their own share. Some Jewish readers hear the righteous within Israel, or the prophet himself, and the ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, reads the passage's opening verse as speaking of the Messiah. Christians read this chapter as speaking of Jesus. The same words, read in different ways by two traditions, each with its own teachers and commentaries. This path follows the Jewish reading, and notice what that reading does. It refuses the onlookers' first conclusion: he must have deserved it. Suffering is not proof of guilt. A people can be despised and still be God's servant. Still be held. Still have a future.

segments.voice: Let one person or one people come to mind who are suffering and are blamed for it, the ones people say must have brought it on themselves. If any part of you has quietly agreed, don't argue with it; just set it down, and stay with them a while, looking instead of turning away, the way the onlookers finally did. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

793.title: The fast I have chosen (Isaiah 58:6–7)
793.hook: read on Yom Kippur: loose the bonds, share your bread, house the poor
793.howItsDone: Isaiah 58 is read as the prophetic reading on Yom Kippur morning, and some Jews mark the day by giving charity or bringing food for those in need as the fast ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Targum and the suffering servant. Your line was the servant is the people. Today, a fast day.

It's the morning of Yom Kippur. The synagogue is full of people who haven't eaten since the evening before. No food, no water, hours of prayer. And in the middle of it, someone stands up to read from the prophets, and the reading is Isaiah fifty-eight, in which God asks, more or less: is this the fast I want? On the fast day itself, the fasting people hear a prophet question their fasting. Some readers think that placement is the whole point.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR MORNING. NO FOOD, NO WATER.` → `THE READING: ISAIAH 58.` → `IS THIS THE FAST I WANT?`

segments.voice: The chapter starts with the people's complaint: "Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?" We did everything right; why isn't God noticing? The prophet answers: on the day of your fast you still chase your own business and push your workers hard. You fast and quarrel. Then comes the turn: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?" What the prophet does not say matters. He doesn't say: stop fasting. Yom Kippur is still a fast, and the people hearing this chapter are still hungry. He says the fast was never only about the empty stomach. It points somewhere: to the person whose stomach is empty without choosing it. And that last phrase: hide not thyself from thine own flesh. Don't look away from another human being, as if they weren't your own family. Going hungry for a day, the chapter suggests, is meant to make a person notice the people who are hungry every day.

794.title: Call the Sabbath a delight (Isaiah 58:13)
794.hook: honor Shabbat by setting your own business aside
794.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat set work and weekday business aside from Friday sundown to Saturday night, marking the day with candles, festive meals, prayer, rest and study; oneg Shabbat, the delight of the Sabbath, is a phrase drawn from this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tsom, the fast God chooses: loose the bonds, open the house. Your line was share thy bread. Today, the same chapter, a few verses on.

Friday night, after services, some synagogues set out a table in the back: cake, tea, fruit, people lingering and talking. It may be called an oneg. A long table of sugar named after a verse of Isaiah. Oneg is the Hebrew word for delight, and it comes from the end of chapter fifty-eight, the same chapter that challenged the fasting people. Having asked for justice alongside the fast, the prophet turns to the seventh day, and doesn't call it a duty or a burden. He says: call it a delight.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT: AN ONEG.` → `ONEG MEANS DELIGHT.` → `SAME CHAPTER AS YESTERDAY.`

segments.voice: The verse, near the chapter's end: "If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable." And it goes on: not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words. At first that sounds like a contradiction. Don't do your own pleasure, and call it a delight? But the Hebrew word the King James gives as pleasure can also mean business, the things you're chasing. The 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it thy business. So: turn your foot away. Step off the road you walk every weekday. Set down what you're pursuing, and in the space that leaves, find delight. The rabbis took even the last phrase seriously: speaking thine own words. In the Talmud, it's read as a guide to Shabbat talk: don't spend the day on deals and errands and the to-do list. Let the conversation rest too. And the verb is call. It's something you name, and naming it changes how it's lived. The same hours can be named a day where nothing gets done, or a day of delight. And the promise at the end: then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord. The delight people give the day comes back to them. For Jews who keep it, that can mean candles, a good meal, a nap, a walk, a long talk at the table.

segments.voice: Look ahead at the next few days and find one hour you could give back: no business, no errands, no to-do list. Ask what would make it a delight and not just a gap: a walk, a meal with someone, a book, a nap, music. If you keep Shabbat, you can think of one new delight to bring to it this week.

795.title: Arise, shine (Isaiah 60:1)
795.hook: "Arise, shine, for thy light is come"
795.carry: the light came before you did
795.howItsDone: Isaiah 60 is among the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and its opening words, kumi ori, are sung on Friday nights in the Shabbat song Lecha Dodi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oneg: set your business aside and call the Sabbath a delight. Your line was call it a delight. Today, a line Shabbat sings.

Wake up, wake up, for your light has come. That line is sung on Friday night in Lecha Dodi, the song that welcomes Shabbat like a bride, in a verse that calls out to a city. Inside it sit two Hebrew words: kumi ori. Arise, shine. They weren't written for the song. The poet borrowed them from Isaiah, from the opening of chapter sixty, where the prophet calls out to a city sitting in the dark.
screen: `WAKE UP, WAKE UP.` → `FRIDAY NIGHT: LECHA DODI.` → `KUMI ORI, BORROWED FROM ISAIAH.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixty opens: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee." The one spoken to is Zion, the city, pictured as a woman. A few chapters earlier, Isaiah told her to shake herself from the dust. Now she's told to stand up. And look at the tense. Thy light is come. Not will come. Not might come if you try hard enough. It has come. The command to rise arrives after the light, not before it. She isn't told to make the morning, only to get up into a morning that's already here. The next verse is honest about the world around her: darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people. The night isn't over everywhere. But the light is on her, in the middle of that darkness, and others will come toward it: nations shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising. And the order matters. Arise comes first, shine second. You can't shine lying down. The first act is simply standing up. That's why the line fits a Friday night so well. The week may have been dark and heavy. The world may still be. But Shabbat has come in, and the song says: get up. Your light is here.

It's here already, and you don't have to earn it; let it land. If you pray, you can hold the verse: arise, shine, for thy light is come.

796.title: A new earth (Isaiah 65:17–25)
796.hook: a vision of no weeping, houses built and lived in, the wolf and lamb at peace
796.carry: nobody's harvest goes to someone else
796.tomorrow: Say not, I am a child (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
796.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah's visions of a repaired world as part of the prophets, and some connect them with tikkun olam, the work of repairing the world through justice and kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kumi ori: stand up into a light that has already come. Your line was the light came before you did. Today, the last day in Isaiah.

A house with someone living in it who also built it. A vineyard where the person who planted the vines gets to drink the wine. A baby who grows up. An old man who lives out all his days. Children who stay with their parents. That's the list. Near the end of Isaiah, the prophet describes a whole new creation, and it turns out to look like an ordinary street on a good afternoon. No golden throne room, no clouds. Just the plain, unbroken things that war and exile kept taking away.
screen: `A HOUSE, BUILT AND LIVED IN.` → `A VINEYARD, PLANTED AND ENJOYED.` → `AN ORDINARY STREET, UNBROKEN.`

segments.voice: It opens big: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind." Then, almost at once, it comes down to street level. Jerusalem will be a joy, and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying. And the heart of it: "And they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them." The next verse says it the other way around: they shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat. For a people who had watched their houses taken and their fields stripped, that is what a new earth means. Not escape from the world. The world, with the theft taken out of it. Your work stays yours. Your children grow up. Then the vision reaches back to an earlier picture in Isaiah, the one from ten days ago: the wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock. And it ends: they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain. The long walk through Isaiah closes on a promise made of ordinary things. Some Jews speak of tikkun olam, repairing the world, as part of the work of moving toward a vision like this one. Different communities hold different hopes for how and when it comes. The text itself keeps it plain: a house, a vine, a long life, and no one hurting anyone on the mountain.

Who lives there safely, who gets to keep what they built, who stops crying? See it in plain detail, and if you pray, you can hold the verse: they shall not hurt nor destroy.

797.title: Say not, I am a child (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
797.hook: the young prophet protests, and God touches his mouth
797.carry: it was never about your size
797.howItsDone: Jeremiah's call is read in synagogue as a haftarah, the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading, in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah closed on a wolf and a lamb feeding together, and your line was nobody's harvest goes to someone else. Today the scroll of Isaiah rolls shut, and a new prophet begins: Jeremiah.

The book of Jeremiah opens with a call, and the first thing the prophet does is say no. The word of the Lord comes to him: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee." Before you were born, I set you apart and made you a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah's answer comes straight back. "Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child." Wrong person, too young, no words. Moses, at the burning bush, made a similar case: I'm slow of speech.
screen: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE, I KNEW THEE.` → `I CANNOT SPEAK.` → `FOR I AM A CHILD.`

segments.voice: The answer begins with the two words that give us today's word. "Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak." The Hebrew word Jeremiah uses for himself is na'ar: a boy, a youth, a young man. The text never tells us his age, and readers have guessed in different directions. What the story cares about is how he sees himself: too small for this. Notice what God doesn't do. He doesn't argue that Jeremiah is older than he thinks, or more gifted, or more ready. No flattery at all. The weight moves somewhere else: you'll go where I send you, and say what I give you. "Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee." Then the call turns physical. The Lord puts out his hand and touches Jeremiah's mouth: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth." Jeremiah named his problem as his mouth, and that's exactly where the touch lands. The call closes with a list of verbs: to root out and to pull down, to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant. Most are about tearing down, and his book will have plenty of that. But the list ends on building and planting. So say not, I am a child isn't a promise that he'll stop feeling small. It's permission to speak anyway, because the words were never supposed to come from his size.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a room where you tend to go quiet, a meeting or a family table where everyone seems older or surer, and find the one thing you'd say there if size didn't matter: a question, a fact, a disagreement, a thank-you. Say it once to yourself, plainly, in your head. If you pray, you can hold the words God said to Jeremiah: say not, I am a child.

798.title: The watching tree (Jeremiah 1:11–12)
798.hook: an almond branch, shaked, sounds like "watching": God watches over the word
798.howItsDone: Jews read the almond-branch vision as part of Jeremiah's opening chapter, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av; Hebrew readers hear the shaked and shoked wordplay directly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prophet said he couldn't speak, and God touched his mouth: it was never about your size. Today, Jeremiah's first vision, and it's a branch.

The next scene opens on a question, the kind a teacher asks: "Jeremiah, what seest thou?" No fire, no throne, no angels with wings. Jeremiah answers with something you could pick up on a hillside. "I see a rod of an almond tree." A stick. A branch from a tree. And God says: you have seen well. The vision is so ordinary that it needs the Hebrew to open it, and inside the Hebrew is a play on words, a serious one.
screen: `WHAT SEEST THOU?` → `A ROD OF AN ALMOND TREE.` → `YOU HAVE SEEN WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the play. The Hebrew word for almond is shaked. God's answer, in the next verse, uses a word that sounds almost the same: shoked, watching, keeping watch. You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it. Shaked, shoked. Almond, watching. In the Hebrew text the two words are written with the same letters; only the vowels differ. So the branch isn't a riddle about trees. It's a sound that carries a promise: the word I give you is not asleep. Some readers add a picture from nature: the almond blossoms early, as if it's awake before the other trees. That's a reader's image, not the verse's, but it fits. In English the pun vanishes. The King James Version has "for I will hasten my word to perform it"; other translations render the word as watching, which at least points back to it. And notice what kind of vision this is. Jeremiah has just been told he'll speak hard words to nations, yet his first lesson isn't in speaking. It's in seeing: look at a plain branch closely enough, and it turns out to be saying something. The same question, what seest thou, comes again in the very next verse. Jeremiah's training starts with his eyes.
screen: `SHAKED, SHOKED: ALMOND, WATCHING.` · then, large: `I WATCH OVER MY WORD.` · then: `THE PUN LOST IN ENGLISH.` · `TRAINING STARTS WITH THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one plain thing near you, a cup, a plant, a shoe by the door, and ask Jeremiah's question quietly: what do I see? Name it plainly, then look a little longer: who made it, who uses it, what has it been through? If nothing comes, the looking is the practice; if you pray, you can hold the verse: I watch over my word.
Shaked. Hebrew for almond, the branch that sounds like shoked, watching: God keeps watch over the word. Today's word.
Your line: look twice, and really see. A plain branch can carry a promise. Day seven hundred ninety-eight, done.
